I refined the hiss under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-nathanialhenniges-Developer-mrdemonwolf-wolf-override/eb713cd4-8931-48d7-8c83-5b0b0d1e9cf3/scratchpad/sound-redo/hiss/refine/ (rec/, synth/B/, scripts/, synth/project/, analysis/). The repository was only read; git status is clean.

The computed task input was cut off partway through the rec candidates, and only the critic's measurement dump (hiss/critic/crit.jsonl plus spectrogram PNGs with no labels) is on disk. I chose the top three and the fixes myself from those critic metrics and my own diagnostics. If the critic picked different ones, this pass needs a re-run against its list.

Top three chosen, by in-game role and critic metrics:
1. hiss_rec_pressure_loop_mid, refined as the whole rec gauge set (low/mid/high), because the game crossfades three gauges and they share one layout.
2. hiss_rec_vent_burst.
3. B-pressure_loop_mid, refined as the whole B gauge set.

The rec coolant_cloud_bed came out of the same build script, so it got the seam fix too. A-coolant_cloud (the 3.0 s one-shot) and A-pressure_loop_high (the strongest whistle flavour) are returned untouched.

Fixes and evidence:
- Recording loops: tonal honk.
  - Found: the +6 dB 845-910 Hz tones in every rec loop come from the air-leak recording #1486 (its own spectrum shows 824-931 Hz at +5..7 dB); they are not in the cooker.
  - Fix: notched the leak before mixing. The 490 Hz tone came from my gurgle EQ (+6 dB Q3), now +2 dB Q1.5.
- Recording loops: seam lull.
  - Found: seam windows sat at -2.44 / -1.44 / -1.0 dB (cloud -3.89) because the wrap fell in a turbulence or billow trough.
  - Fix: rotated each loop to a median-level point with a minimal wrap step. One rotation is shared by all three gauges so they stay in sync. Seams are now -1.33 / -0.49 / 0.00 / -0.14 dB.
- Recording high gauge.
  - Found: 46% of the energy sat in 3-5 kHz, with the third-octave peak at 4 kHz, and this gauge plays at the loudest level.
  - Fix: now 30%, peak at 2 kHz, centroid 3108 -> 2603 Hz.
- Recording vent.
  - Found: 2-3 kHz held 56% of the energy (narrow honk); the #0138 crack carried an 8.2-9.2 kHz whine (+13..15 dB); and the body reached full level 0.3 s after the pop because the source swells.
  - Fix: 2-3 kHz is now 39% (1-2 kHz up to 33%), 5k+ fell from 4.7% to 1.8%, and the blast is at full flow at 0.2-0.4 s.
- Recipe B.
  - Fix 1: 5k+ cut from 9-14% to 3-8%.
  - Fix 2: sub-200 Hz on the low gauge halved (4.8 -> 2.3%).
  - Fix 3: the hole tone now starts earlier, so the mid gauge has an audible tone (1475 Hz +4 dB) and the three gauges differ by more than brightness.
  - Seam: not changed. The critic's seam-flux flag on B (p97) is not a defect. Across five seeds the original B scored p58-p99 with no consistent position. The metric takes the maximum over the 4 frames that straddle the wrap, so a perfect seam scores about the 80th percentile on average. Read every seam_flux_pctile in this set with that in mind.

ranking.why: The best-balanced loop of the 20. It has real steam texture (flatness 0.14, coloured rather than white), 96% of its energy in 200 Hz-5 kHz, a 2.1 kHz centroid and a phone-speaker loss of only -0.7 dB. The seam is effectively perfect (wrap step 0.01x the median step; 40 ms seam level at the 22nd percentile). The envelope moves enough to sound alive (20 ms range 5.2 dB, std 1.6 dB). Weakness: the 'valve whistle' is buried, since no tone at 1390 Hz rises above the local median, so the gauge has to come only from EQ and level.
ranking.fix: Raise the 1390 Hz resonant whistle from 0.1x to about 0.18x hiss RMS so it sits 4-5 dB above the noise. That way mid is audibly between a no-whistle low and a whistling high.

ranking.why: The cleanest synth seam (wrap step 0.01x median, spectral flux across the seam at the 50th percentile). The hole tone hops between about 1.8 and 2.8 kHz at a moderate +5-6 dB, which gives pitch identity without one fixed piercing line. It keeps 86% of its energy in 200 Hz-5 kHz, loses -0.4 dB on a phone and has fast shimmer modulation, so it is the least static of the high-gauge loops. This loop plays loudest (near -8 dB), so it matters most.
ranking.fix: Lower the 8.5 kHz low-pass to about 7 kHz (13.6% of the energy is above 5 kHz). That softens the fizz on headphones at -8 dB without touching the hopping tone.

ranking.why: The only cloud that fits both the 3.0 s DropArm window and the speaker target. Its centroid is 1.9 kHz, it loses -1.2 dB on a phone, only 1.6% of its energy is below 200 Hz and it has no whistle. The puff onset is soft (2 ms from -84 dB), it stays near -19 dBFS until 2.3 s, then fades smoothly to exact zero. No clicks were detected.
ranking.fix: Start the smoothstep fade-out at 2.2 s instead of 1.9 s, so the cloud stays at full body for most of its 3 s on screen (the level is already -24 dB at 2.4 s).

ranking.why: The densest and most convincing release. Whole-clip RMS is -22.8 dBFS (3-4 dB louder than the synth vents), and the pressure fall is clear: the centroid drops from 4.1 kHz at the pop to 1.6 kHz in the tail. The tail decays cleanly to -84 dB with exact-zero edges, and the sputter grains read as distinct spits in the spectrogram. Weaknesses: 56% of the energy sits in one 2-3 kHz band (flatness 0.022, so it can sound honky or resonant), and there are narrow +11 dB peaks at 8.1-8.8 kHz. The first grain also rises 37 dB in 1 ms, the sharpest onset of the vents.
ranking.fix: Add a 4 ms raised-cosine fade-in to each sputter grain, and cut the 2.4 kHz +3 dB presence boost to 0 dB (or apply a -3 dB peak at 2.5 kHz, Q 1.5) so the spectrum spreads out.

ranking.why: It has the strongest gauge identity: a 2143 Hz whistle at +12.2 dB with a 4.46 kHz overtone, right where phone speakers are loudest. But the envelope is the most static of the set (20 ms range 2.4 dB, std 0.77 dB). That leaves a fixed pure tone over steady noise, played continuously at up to -8 dB, which is a fatigue risk. crit.overall:
This review is from measurements only. Nobody has listened, played it in the game or tried it on a phone. I re-measured all 20 candidates with my own tool, independently of the generators: spectrum bands, centroid, tonal prominence, flatness, a phone model (2x high-pass at 500 Hz) and a laptop model (2x high-pass at 200 Hz), the 20 ms envelope, a click detector, and seam step, seam level and spectral flux at the seam. I also looked at spectrograms of the x3 tiled loops and of the one-shots.

**What holds for every candidate**
- Peaks are at -6 dBFS.
- One-shot edges are exact zero.
- Nothing has meaningful energy below 40 Hz.
- No clicks were detected inside the loops.
- Every loop seam is at noise level by sample step.

**Where the candidates differ**
- **Movement.** The synth A and C loops are static: their 20 ms envelope range is 2.2-3.4 dB. Synth B and the recorded (rec) loops move: 4-7 dB. A static loop is the risk Nathanial is most likely to dislike, because it is close to the old shaped-white-noise hiss.
- **Gauge identity.** Recipe A has the clearest whistle progression, from +4 dB at low to +12 dB at high, but +12 dB is likely piercing when it plays at -8 dB. The rec loops' whistles are buried below detection.
- **Phone speakers.** All of recipe C, B-low and B-cloud lose 2-4 dB on the phone model and lean toward rumble.

**Recommended set**
- **Pressure loops:** the three gauge loops must come from one family so the game can crossfade them. The rec family (low, mid, high) or the B family (low, mid, high) are the best choices. Within the families, rec-mid and B-high are the best single loops.
- **Vent:** rec vent_burst, or B-vent if it has to stay code-generated.
- **Cloud:** A-coolant_cloud, the only cloud that is shaped to 3.0 s and in range on a phone.

**Before choosing, Nathanial should know two costs**
- **Synth:** at 44.1 kHz it breaks the 400 ms startup budget in tests/sfx_bank_test.gd. Each 6 s loop takes 1.1-1.9 s to generate, so it needs generating on a background worker or rendering at 22.05 kHz.
- **Rec:** the sources are BigSoundBank 0805, 1486 and 0138, which I confirmed as CC0 on the saved pages. They would ship as baked WAV assets with entries in the asset register, rather than as code in SfxBank. The 22 kHz rec copies have worse seams than the 44.1 kHz masters (the low copy's wrap level step is 2.8 dB), so ship the 44.1 kHz masters or resample them seam-aware.

**What to listen for first**
- The x3 tiled files, for the seam swell in recipe A (95-99th percentile) and the seam dip in the rec low loop and the cloud bed.
- How loud A-high's 2.1 kHz whistle is.
- Whether B-low's 9 Hz chuff sounds like a leak or like an engine.

crit.overall:
Critic pass on the arc. I judged from measurements and spectrograms only; nobody has listened to these and nothing was played in the game. I re-measured all 12 candidates plus the current arc, whine and clank with my own stdlib analyser. It covers bands, a phone filter (high-pass 300 Hz at 24 dB/oct, low-pass 7 kHz), the loudest 50 ms, 10 ms envelopes, how strongly the level pulses at 120 Hz in the 300 Hz+ band, narrow tonal peaks and spectrogram/waveform PNGs. Results are in .../scratchpad/sound-redo/arc/critic/m.json, the PNGs in critic/png/ and the tools in critic/tools/ (arcrit.py, seg.py). The repo was only read.

Every candidate passes the basics: peak -6.02 dBFS, first and last samples exactly 0, DC under 0.0004, no clipped samples, nothing below 40 Hz, and 78-97% of the energy in 200 Hz-5 kHz. The phone filter costs at most 2.2 dB.

**Biggest problem, which all four bolt candidates share:** in main.gd, `_bolt_arc()` plays `arc` at the moment the whine ends. The flash, the camera shake, the spark burst and the clank (pitch 0.7) all fire then too. The whine already builds for 0.6 s: it rises from -32 to -11 dB and from 320 Hz to 1.6 kHz. So a bolt clip with a 0.5-0.55 s build:
- puts its crack 0.5-0.55 s after the flash;
- plays a second build after the first one.

The fix is either to put the crack about 6 ms into the clip, or to start the clip 0.5 s before the whine ends (when `bolt_charge_remaining <= crack_at`).

**Loudness:** the synth clips have a crest of 12-16 dB and their loudest 50 ms sits at -11 to -14 dBFS. The recorded clips have a crest of 18-21 dB and sit at -17 to -20 dBFS, about the same as the current arc (-18.7), so they barely fix its quietness.

**Mains identity** (share of the level pulsing at 120 Hz):
- B: 0.51-0.70, the clearest.
- Recorded: 0.26-0.36.
- A: 0.10-0.16.
- C: about 0.05 (its timing is free-running).

**A mistake in the synth notes:** their caution 4 is wrong. At 22.05 kHz the bank only loses what is above 11 kHz, which is at most 0.7% of these clips. 5-11 kHz survives, so every synth clip could be rendered at the bank's 22.05 kHz with no audible loss.

**Best per slot:**
- Records exit: B_records, with A_records as the alternative.
- Relay: A_relay or C_relay. Both are designed for pitch 1.0, but main.gd plays the relay arc at pitch 1.2 and -8 dB under a 0 dB clank.
- Exit bolt: B_bolt, but only once the timing is fixed.

Recipes B and A are the strongest families. C is the most stylised and the weakest fit next to the whine. The recorded clips sound real but are quiet, still 19-21% above 5 kHz, and shipping them would break the bank's "no third-party audio" claim and need asset-register entries. The ranking crosses slots and is by how close each clip is to shippable where it is used.

ranking.why: Records exit (plays at -3 dB together with the flash): the crack at 6 ms is in sync with the flash. Its level pulses clearly at 120 Hz (share 0.51, envelope peak exactly 120 Hz), so it reads as a mains arc on any speaker. 95% of the energy is in 200 Hz-5 kHz and the phone filter costs only 0.7 dB. The decay is smooth from -15 to -57 dB, and the restrike at 0.15 s (-14 dB) is distinct. Flaws: the housing modes leave a narrow tone at 1723 Hz, 8.8 dB above its neighbours, ringing for about 0.17 s, and one stray spit at 0.51-0.52 s sits about 10 dB above the -51 dB tail.
ranking.fix: Shorten the housing-mode decays in _b_crack to 12 ms or less and halve the send to the Q 9 resonators, so the 1723 Hz line stops ringing by about 60 ms and the crack stays a crack rather than a 'ting'.

ranking.why: The warmest clip and the loudest at the same peak: its loudest 50 ms is -12.6 dBFS, against -16.9 for the recorded Records clip and -18.7 for the current arc. It has 38.5% in 300 Hz-1 kHz, which directly fixes the 'no body' complaint about the current arc. Clean edges, crack at 9 ms, restrike at 0.15 s, smooth tail. Weak points: the 120 Hz buzz shows as steady harmonic lines, so it sounds like transformer hum under noise rather than a pulsing arc (120 Hz share only 0.095). The tanh drive also packs the first 0.15 s into a dense block at about -13 dB.
ranking.fix: Multiply the buzz and sizzle by B's reignition envelope (|sin(2*pi*60t)|^4 at about 0.6 depth) during the 0.1 s buzz hold, so the hum pulses at 120 Hz like a live arc rather than sitting steady.

ranking.why: Relay contact (plays at -8 dB, pitch 1.2, under a 0 dB clank that lasts 40 ms): it has hum identity (120 Hz share 0.14), an even noise spread (spectral flatness 0.57) and a restrike at 55 ms that lands after the clank has died. Its level at 50-120 ms is -16 to -25 dB, so the spark is heard after the clank. But it was designed for pitch 1.0. At the current pitch 1.2 its 12% above 5 kHz shifts up and it gets brighter again. At -8 dB its loudest 50 ms is about -22 dBFS against the clank's -18.8, and the snap at 4 ms is hidden under the clank.
ranking.fix: Change the call in main.gd (the relay contact, line 1884) from play(&"arc", -8.0, 1.2) to about play(&"arc", -5.0, 1.0), so it plays at its designed pitch and with 3 dB more level to clear the clank.

ranking.why: The best separation from the clank: 69% in 1-5 kHz where the clank has little (the clank is 68% in 300 Hz-1 kHz), and distinct stutter bursts at 0.09, 0.15 and 0.21 s that stand clear of the clank's 40 ms as a 'zzt-zzt'. The loudest 50 ms is -14.2 dBFS, and the phone filter costs only 0.8 dB. But it has no mains periodicity at all (120 Hz share 0.045), so it does not match the 120 Hz identity of the other two arcs. Its highest narrow peak is up at 6.4 kHz. The stylised FM 'pew' can read as a laser rather than a relay contact.
ranking.fix: Lock the stutter gate and the crackle grains to the 120 Hz half-cycles, as A and B do (open the gate on the |sin(2*pi*60t)| peaks), so it shares the mains identity of the other arcs while keeping its stutter.

ranking.why: A real recorded crackle texture with genuine 120 Hz gating (share 0.26, envelope peak 120 Hz). The phone filter costs only 0.6 dB, and there is a believable second snap at 175 ms. But its crest is 18.1 dB and its loudest 50 ms is -16.9 dBFS, 4-5 dB below the synth Records clips at the same peak, which only partly fixes the old quietness. 18.9% of its energy is still in 5-8 kHz (centroid 2.7 kHz), part of the 'too bright' fault being replaced. ranking.why: Loud (loudest 50 ms -12.3 dBFS, crest 14.1 dB) and punchy, with a clear restrike at 0.15 s (-12 dB). In game, though, the crack lands at 0.50 s, half a second after _bolt_arc's flash, shake, spark burst and clank, and the 0.5 s build plays after the whine has already built. The crack (-11 dB) is only about 6 dB above the end of the build (-17 dB). The housing modes ring as horizontal lines (1.7, 2.6 and 3.9 kHz) for about 0.1 s after the crack.

Its loudest 50 ms is only -18.9 dBFS (crest 20.6 dB), the same quietness as the current arc. 20.6% is in 5-8 kHz, and the build has a 12 dB hole around 5-5.6 kHz plus 97/194 Hz lines from the synthetic forceField layer. After 40 ms it only reaches -24 to -30 dB before the -8 dB call gain. At pitch 1.2 its 10% in 5-8 kHz moves up toward the harsh band.

ranking.fix: Cut the housing-mode decays to 5-10 ms and drop the 1150 Hz mode for this plan, so the relay is a dry tick and arc buzz and stops doubling the clank's metal ring.

crit.overall:
I checked these by measurement, not by listening (headless renders and numbers only): my own band, envelope and spectrogram measurements, a simulated phone speaker (300 Hz high-pass plus 7 kHz low-pass) and a laptop speaker (150 Hz high-pass), 20-40 Hz rasp after the phone filter, spectral movement and a high-frequency click count. Neither track wins outright. The recordings sound more alive: their tone colour moves over time (centroid variation 0.20-0.36 against 0.05-0.22 for the synth clips), they lose only 1.2-1.7 dB through a phone and they have no clicks in the seam and assertive takes. But all three are thin below 200 Hz (0.6-5.3%) with pitch at 112-278 Hz, so WOLF can sound small on headphones. The warning recording also ends abruptly: the second snarl is still at full level (overall RMS peak at 1.09 s) when the 110 ms fade cuts it off. The synth clips are deep and clean, with proper die-aways (-35 to -43 dB in the last 100 ms). Recipe C is clearly the best of them. A and B hold a flat level for the whole body and keep a fixed pulse grid, so on a phone they risk the same synth-buzz problem as the old growl. B's 6-bit crush adds 26-55 HF ticks/s, and its servo whistles sit above the voice.

Recommendation:
- **Seam:** rec-seam, with a lower varispeed and a low shelf to add size.
- **Lane-choice warning:** synth C-warning. It needs no third-party audio and fits the code-generated audio direction, but give it a rise-dip-snarl contour first. Alternatively, re-trim rec-warning so it ends on a natural decay, then compare the two.
